items.title: [Bug]: chatgpt/ device-code auth is synchronous and blocks the proxy event loop for up to 900s, killing the worker
items.body:
- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. Searched `is:issue "device code"` — 9 results, none reports this. #27175, #24562 and #17065 are different faults. ### What happened? A single request for a `chatgpt/*` model froze both of our proxy replicas for ~6.5 minutes each, until Kubernetes killed them. The proxy stopped answering every request, including `/health/liveliness`, and emitted no log output at all for the duration. The cause is that ChatGPT's device-code login is synchronous, and it is reached from an `async def` request handler: ``` async def async_response_api_handler() llms/custom_httpx/llm_http_handler.py:2730 → provider_config.validate_environment() llm_http_handler.py:2764 ← plain def, runs inline on the loop → ChatGPTResponsesConfig.validate_environment() llms/chatgpt/responses/transformation.py:41 → Authenticator.get_access_token() llms/chatgpt/authenticator.py:43 → _login_device_code() authenticator.py:143 → print(device code to stdout) authenticator.py:152 → _poll_for_authorization_code() authenticator.py:199 _get_httpx_client() :200 ← sync client while time.time() - start < DEVICE_CODE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS: :203 time.sleep(...) :224, :230, :241 ``` The budget is set by the constants at `authenticator.py:25-28`: | Constant | Value | | --- | --- | | `DEVICE_CODE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `15 * 60` — 900 s | | `DEVICE_CODE_POLL_SLEEP_SECONDS` | `5` | | `DEVICE_CODE_COOLDOWN_SECONDS` | `5 * 60` | So one request can hold the event loop for up to 900 seconds. `_wait_for_access_token()` (`:362`, `while` at `:364`, `time.sleep` at `:373`) does the same for a second request arriving inside the cooldown. ```mermaid flowchart TD R["POST /v1/responses, model chatgpt/*"] --> H["async def async_response_api_handler()"] H --> V["validate_environment() — sync, no await point"] V --> P["device-code poll loop
time.sleep, up to 900 s"] P -.->|"event loop never yields"| S["starved on the same thread"] S --> S1["/health/liveliness and /health/readiness
never dispatched → orchestrator kills the worker"] S2["every other in-flight request"] --- S S3["uvicorn's own access log → total silence"] --- S ``` Three things turn this from slow into fatal on a proxy: 1. `validate_environment` is part of the sync provider-config interface. Every other provider returns headers in microseconds; this one waits on a human. Network I/O with sleeps does not belong behind a synchronous interface method. 2. It blocks during header construction, *before* any call to the model — so the model name after the prefix is irrelevant, and every `chatgpt/*` model is affected. 3. With `NUM_WORKERS=1` there is no sibling worker to answer the health probe, so the container fails its liveness check and is killed. Our probe error was `Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers` — the TCP connection was accepted, but no HTTP response ever came. This is not a one-time setup problem. The token file lives at `~/.config/litellm/chatgpt/auth.json` inside the container, so it is lost on every restart, and `_is_token_expired` re-arms the flow whenever the token expires. `llms/github_copilot/authenticator.py` has the same shape — sync `_get_httpx_client()`, `time.sleep(5)` at `:325`, `print(` at `:349` — so a fix should probably cover both. **What I expected instead:** a request that cannot authenticate returns an error promptly. A server should never print an interactive prompt to stdout, and should never block its event loop waiting for one to be answered. Either refuse the device flow when no TTY/interactive session exists and return a clear "ChatGPT auth not configured, run the login flow first" error, or run it in a thread with a short timeout so the loop keeps serving. ### User Flow **Before a (hypothetical) fix** — one user's request takes the proxy offline for everyone until the container is restarted. 1. User A sends `POST https:///v1/responses` with `{"model": "chatgpt/gpt-5.6-terra", "input": "hi"}` and a valid virtual key. 2. The request never returns. User A's client hangs with no status code and no error. 3. User B sends `POST https:///v1/messages` with a Claude model that has always worked. It returns `503 Service Unavailable` from the load balancer in front of the proxy. 4. User B sends `GET https:///health/liveliness`. The connection is accepted but no response headers ever arrive; the client times out. 5. This continues for ~6.5 minutes across ~300 requests from other users, all `503`. 6. The container is killed and restarted. Requests then succeed again, and User A's original request is gone with no response. 7. Any user holding a valid key can repeat step 1 at will and take the proxy down for every other user. **After a (hypothetical) fix** — the same request fails on its own and nobody else notices. 1. User A sends `POST https:///v1/responses` with `{"model": "chatgpt/gpt-5.6-terra", "input": "hi"}` and a valid virtual key. 2. The request returns promptly with an error explaining that ChatGPT authentication has not been completed for this deployment. 3. User B sends `POST https:///v1/messages` with the same Claude model. It returns `200 OK`. 4. User B sends `GET https:///health/liveliness`. It returns `200 OK`. 5. No other request is affected, and nothing is logged as an outage. 6. The container is not restarted. 7. A user holding a valid key can no longer affect any other user's requests. ### Proof the bug occurs **Setup.** Proxy on Kubernetes, one replica set of 2 pods, `NUM_WORKERS=1`, `litellm-gateway:v1.99.0`. Relevant config (models unrelated to the trigger removed, credentials redacted): ```yaml general_settings: store_model_in_db: true master_key: litellm_settings: callbacks: [...] model_list: - model_name: gpt-5.6-terra litellm_params: model: bedrock/openai.gpt-5.6-terra aws_region_name: us-east-1 model_info: mode: responses use_openai_responses_path: true ``` Liveness probe: `/health/liveliness`, `periodSeconds: 15`, `timeoutSeconds: 10`, `failureThreshold: 6`. Readiness probe: `/health/readiness`, `periodSeconds: 10`, `timeoutSeconds: 10`, `failureThreshold: 3`. No `chatgpt/*` model was in `model_list`. This was not a synthetic test — it is a production incident, and I have not re-run it deliberately because doing so takes the gateway offline. **Step 1-2 — the request that hangs.** A developer ran `codex --model chatgpt/gpt-5.6-terra` against the proxy. Both pods printed this to stdout within 533 ms of each other, with a different code each, and then went completely silent. Note there is no access-log line for the triggering request, because uvicorn logs only on completion: ``` 2026-09-02T15:23:37.192Z Sign in with ChatGPT using device code: 2026-09-02T15:23:37.192Z 1) Visit https://auth.openai.com/codex/device 2026-09-02T15:23:37.192Z 2) Enter code: XXXX-XXXXX 2026-09-02T15:23:37.192Z Device codes are a common phishing target. Never share this code. ``` Log output per pod, showing the gap — normal traffic right up to the prompt, then nothing until the replacement process boots: ``` pod A: 513 events 15:20:03 → 15:32:58, largest gap 403.8 s (15:23:37 → 15:30:20) pod B: 378 events 15:20:00 → 15:32:59, largest gap 410.9 s (15:23:37 → 15:30:28) ``` **Step 3 — other users get 503.** Load-balancer metrics per minute. `ELB_5XX` is generated by the load balancer itself; `Target_5XX` is what the proxy returned: ``` minute ELB_5XX ELB_503 Target_5XX TargetConnectionError 15:24 30 30 - - 15:25 22 22 - - 15:26 63 63 - - 15:27 45 45 - - 15:28 41 40 - - 15:29 65 65 - - 15:30 36 36 - - ``` `Target_5XX` and `TargetConnectionError` are empty for the whole window: the proxy returned nothing, so all ~301 errors were synthesised by the load balancer once both targets had dropped out of rotation. **Step 4 — health endpoints stop answering.** From the orchestrator, for both pods: ``` Liveness probe failed: Get "http://:4000/health/liveliness": context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers) Readiness probe failed: Get "http://:4000/health/readiness": context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers) ``` The connection was accepted and no headers came, i.e. the process was alive with a stalled loop. For contrast, a pod that was genuinely shutting down later reported `connect: connection refused`. **Step 6 — the container is killed.** Container state after the event, both pods: ``` reason=Error exit=137 (SIGKILL from the failed liveness probe, not OOMKilled) pod A: died 15:30:08, restarted 15:30:08, back up 15:30:20 pod B: died 15:30:15, restarted 15:30:15, back up 15:30:28 ``` The kill arrived at ~400 s, i.e. it interrupted the 900 s poll budget less than half way through. **Line references** were verified against the `litellm==1.99.0` wheel from PyPI, not the `main` branch. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.99.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details No response

gold.rationale: The synchronous device-code auth flow blocks the async event loop for up to 900 seconds, causing the entire proxy worker to become unresponsive, failing health checks and causing the container to be killed. This affects all requests across all providers/users on the same worker, not just chatgpt users — a single malicious or unaware user with a valid key can take down the whole proxy for everyone. This is a clear violation of expected behavior (async handlers should not block the event loop), matching the bug category. It affects the shared core request-handling path (event loop blocking impacts all providers, not just chatgpt), which per modifiers raises severity by one level. There's no reasonable workaround short of avoiding the chatgpt provider entirely, and the impact is a full outage for all users on that worker — this is P0-level (broken for most users on a release, no real workaround, akin to a DoS vector). Even without formally being a security CVE, it is effectively an unauthenticated-by-any-valid-key denial-of-service vector affecting the whole service; however per rules, since it's framed and diagnosed as a bug (blocking sync call in async handler) rather than an exploit of an auth bypass or injection, it fits best as 'bug' rather than 'security', though the severity should be treated with urgency and needs_human due to the systemic impact. Given the severity (worker-killing, no workaround, affects all users on same worker, potential DoS), this warrants P0 urgency and needs_human=true for maintainer judgement on the architectural fix (thread offload vs. disabling interactive flow).

items.title: Request for maintainer review: pinned LiteLLM 1.99.0 conformance measurements
items.body:
I maintain a small OpenAI-compatible HTTP conformance benchmark and measured two pinned LiteLLM configurations. I’m asking you to check my configuration, interpretation, and raw artifact.

I wrote the benchmark and maintain LLM-Shield-Proxy, one of the gateways it measures, so I have an obvious conflict of interest. Each row below is one maintainer-produced run and is unreplicated. I am asking for corrections or a reproduction, not endorsement.

### What I ran
```
model_list:
  - model_name: conformance-model
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/conformance-model
      api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8765/v1
      api_key: <controlled-capture-key>

general_settings:
  master_key: <local-evaluation-key>

litellm_settings:
  telemetry: false
  set_verbose: false
```

For the Presidio run, the same base configuration plus:
```
guardrails:
  - guardrail_name: presidio-pii-masking
    litellm_params:
      guardrail: presidio
      mode: pre_call
      output_parse_pii: true
      default_on: true
```
```
PRESIDIO_ANALYZER_API_BASE=http://127.0.0.1:5002
PRESIDIO_ANONYMIZER_API_BASE=http://127.0.0.1:5001
Presidio analyzer score_threshold: 0.0
```

```
mcr.microsoft.com/presidio-analyzer@sha256:286e3fa7f3a7426e775e8564fe1870f1ba8f999d3ab8bbb8cc46a44355d9d6e9
mcr.microsoft.com/presidio-anonymizer@sha256:a10a12a2a613d13cf29d3ad3641e3258444dd8c90403dd644a0a114c472c2483
```

**Is this the correct way to configure LiteLLM 1.99.0 for Presidio masking and client-side restoration through output_parse_pii?**
- `litellm[proxy]==1.99.0` on CPython 3.12.3
- Local loopback capture, three iterations
- Default configuration with no PII guardrail attached
- Presidio configuration using the stock analyzer and anonymizer images pinned by digest, the stock recognizer registry, no ad-hoc recognizers, and `score_threshold: 0.0`
- Presidio guardrail settings included `mode: pre_call`, `default_on: true`, and `output_parse_pii: true`

Three iterations are a conformance smoke test, not a performance benchmark. I am making no speed or latency claim.

### Result summary

The default configuration had no PII guardrail attached. Its outcome is `redaction-not-enabled`: a statement about that configuration, not a verdict about LiteLLM.

With Presidio enabled, `leaked_entity_types` was empty: no protected fixture value reached the configured capture upstream. The outcome is `no-leak-profile-not-met` because this profile requires the original values to be restored to the client, while the measured path behaved as one-way anonymization. This is not a privacy failure.

All links below are pinned to merged PR #22’s head commit, `1e1f72846e071367c23521d2b7bffbde639c39d4`:

- [Configuration record](https://github.com/ninadphalak/LLM-Shield-Proxy/blob/1e1f72846e071367c23521d2b7bffbde639c39d4/benchmarks/results/http-profile-litellm-1.99.0.md)
- [Default raw artifact](https://github.com/ninadphalak/LLM-Shield-Proxy/blob/1e1f72846e071367c23521d2b7bffbde639c39d4/benchmarks/results/http-profile-litellm-1.99.0-default.json) — SHA-256 `dd107de45abd3ef6cf9c3c6f6e6b200e8bf7c8c8a82b932f2128d0f4b296c21c`
- [Presidio raw artifact](https://github.com/ninadphalak/LLM-Shield-Proxy/blob/1e1f72846e071367c23521d2b7bffbde639c39d4/benchmarks/results/http-profile-litellm-1.99.0-presidio.json) — SHA-256 `f660fa5b21ce2bdb705b83db1c513ad64aa5392c0c37600e2215fbd131621486`
- [HTTP-profile methodology](https://github.com/ninadphalak/LLM-Shield-Proxy/blob/1e1f72846e071367c23521d2b7bffbde639c39d4/website/docs/conformance/index.md)
- [Fixture threat model](https://github.com/ninadphalak/LLM-Shield-Proxy/blob/1e1f72846e071367c23521d2b7bffbde639c39d4/website/docs/conformance/fixture-threat-model.md)
- [Report schema](https://github.com/ninadphalak/LLM-Shield-Proxy/blob/1e1f72846e071367c23521d2b7bffbde639c39d4/spec/v1.0.0/http-profile.schema.json)
- [Reproduction instructions](https://github.com/ninadphalak/LLM-Shield-Proxy/blob/1e1f72846e071367c23521d2b7bffbde639c39d4/website/docs/conformance/reproducing.md)

Could you please check three things?

1. Is the pinned LiteLLM and Presidio configuration representative and complete?
2. Is my interpretation of `output_parse_pii: true` fair, or did I configure or invoke the restoration path incorrectly?
3. Given the raw artifacts, are `redaction-not-enabled` and `no-leak-profile-not-met` fair outcome classifications?

If anything is wrong, please tell me what to correct or provide a reproduction that reaches a different result. I will correct the public record.

gold.rationale: This is a well-researched, self-disclosed conflict-of-interest report asking maintainers to review a third-party benchmark's methodology and interpretation regarding LiteLLM's Presidio guardrail configuration and output_parse_pii behavior. The author is not claiming a definitive bug ("This is not a privacy failure") but asking for validation of configuration correctness and interpretation - essentially "did I configure this correctly / is my interpretation fair?" This fits the question category best: the author is asking how the output_parse_pii restoration path is supposed to work and whether their config is correct, not asserting with confidence that the software misbehaves. However, there's an underlying plausible claim that output_parse_pii restoration isn't working as documented, which could indicate a real gap between documented behavior and actual behavior - but the author explicitly frames this as uncertainty about their own configuration, not a confident bug claim. Given the explicit request for maintainer judgement on interpretation and correctness, and the complexity/ambiguity requiring maintainer expertise to adjudicate, this needs human review. It's a narrow, niche request (single reporter, self-benchmark, unreplicated) affecting a specific guardrail configuration path, not a widespread issue, so urgency is low (P3). But because it requires judgement to interpret whether the behavior matches documentation and there's a conflict of interest requiring careful handling, needs_human should be true.

items.title: [Bug]: Team/user/key budget reset job silently defaults an unparseable budget_duration (e.g. "") to a daily reset
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

If a team (or user/key) row has `budget_duration` set to an empty string `""` (as opposed to `null`), LiteLLM's periodic reset job (`ResetBudgetJob`) — and the `/team/new` creation path itself — treats this as a "provided" duration and computes a reset schedule for it, which silently resolves to **"reset every 24 hours at midnight UTC"**, even though `""` was never intended to mean "daily." This wipes `spend` every 24 hours on any row that ends up with `budget_duration=""`, with no error and no way to reject the value up front.

Root cause: in `litellm/litellm_core_utils/duration_parser.py`, `get_next_standardized_reset_time` does:

    value, unit = _parse_duration(_normalize_duration(duration))
    if value is None:
        # Fall back to default if format is invalid
        return current_time.replace(hour=0, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0) + timedelta(days=1)

`_parse_duration("")` can't match its regex against an empty string and returns `(None, None)`, so this silently computes "next midnight" instead of raising or treating the value as "no reset." The same fallback is reached with no validation in between from both `litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/team_endpoints.py::new_team` (computes `budget_reset_at` at creation time whenever `budget_duration is not None`, true for `""`) and `ResetBudgetJob._reset_budget_common` on every scheduler tick. No `field_validator` exists on any `budget_duration` field in `litellm/proxy/_types.py`, so `""` is never rejected at the API layer.

As of a recent version, this fallback also logs a `WARNING` ("Unrecognized budget_duration %r; falling back to a next-midnight reset...") — but the behavior itself is unchanged.

**Related issues:** #17993 is a different bug in the same file (`duration_parser.py`) — a day-rollover miscalculation for large second/minute/hour duration values — not a duplicate of this one, which is about an *unparseable* value (`""`) being silently accepted rather than rejected.


### User Flow

Before a (hypothetical) fix: an admin creates a team meaning it to never auto-reset, and it ends up on a silent daily reset instead.

1. Admin calls POST https://<proxy-domain>/team/new with body {"team_alias": "my-team", "budget_duration": ""}.
2. The response comes back HTTP 200 immediately, with "budget_duration": "" and "budget_reset_at" already set to next midnight UTC (e.g. "2026-09-03T00:00:00Z") — no error, even though a daily reset was never requested.
3. The next day, the admin calls GET https://<proxy-domain>/team/info?team_id=<id> and sees "spend": 0 — all of the team's accumulated spend is gone, and "budget_reset_at" has rolled forward to the following midnight.
4. This repeats every 24 hours indefinitely; the team's spend field never reflects more than one day of usage.

After a (hypothetical) fix: an empty/unparseable budget_duration is rejected or treated as "never reset."

1. Admin calls POST https://<proxy-domain>/team/new with the same body {"team_alias": "my-team", "budget_duration": ""}.
2. Either the request comes back with a 4xx validation error naming budget_duration, so the admin corrects it before the team is created — or the team is created with "budget_duration": null and "budget_reset_at": null, the same state as leaving the field blank.
3. GET https://<proxy-domain>/team/info?team_id=<id> the next day, and every day after, shows spend accumulating normally with no silent reset.

### Proof the bug occurs

Config the proxy ran with (general_settings/litellm_settings/model_list omitted here as not relevant to this bug — a minimal config with any working model_list reproduces this):

  general_settings:
    master_key: sk-local-test

Version: v1.97.0 (also confirmed unchanged on v1.83.10-stable and v1.84.10)

Commands and full output:

  $ curl -sf -X POST http://localhost:4000/team/new \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-**" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"team_alias": "issue1-empty-duration-test", "budget_duration": ""}'
  {
    "team_id": "1c8c0ae8-21c6-4d3a-9759-d78633e9dc3e",
    "team_alias": "issue1-empty-duration-test",
    "budget_duration": "",
    "budget_reset_at": "2026-09-03T00:00:00Z"
  }

Container log line confirming the fallback fired at creation time:

  18:17:57 - LiteLLM:WARNING: duration_parser.py:141 - Unrecognized budget_duration ''; falling back to a next-midnight reset. Use the <int><unit> format (e.g. '1h', '7d', '30d', '1mo').

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.97.0

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: The code violates the intended contract: an unparseable budget_duration ("") should not silently produce a daily reset schedule. This causes real data loss (spend wiped every 24 hours) with no error, affecting team/user/key budget tracking across the shared core duration_parser path used by multiple endpoints (team, user, key, scheduler). This is a clear bug (docs/contract violated by code), not just a docs issue, since it causes silent data loss. It affects the shared core path (duration_parser + reset job), which is used broadly, and there's no workaround for the affected row once created except manual intervention. This warrants raising urgency due to core path impact and data loss potential, but it's a narrower trigger (only affects rows with budget_duration="") so not P0. It requires a judgement call on whether to reject at API level vs. treat as null, so a maintainer should decide the correct fix approach.

items.title: [Bug]: OpenAI reasoning-model prompt cache never carries forward through /v1/messages → Responses API bridge (encrypted_content dropped, even after #37953)
items.body:
## Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

## What happened?

When a client speaks Anthropic's `/v1/messages` protocol (e.g. Claude Code) and LiteLLM bridges that to an OpenAI **reasoning** model via the Responses API, prompt caching for the reasoning portion never hits across turns. Every turn re-prices as a cold cache miss for the reasoning tokens, no matter how long the conversation runs.

This is **not** the same bug as #24985 / #24425 / #36197 (all closed, fixed by #37953). Those fixed thinking blocks being flattened into visible assistant text (a correctness/leak bug). This issue is about **prompt-cache continuity** specifically, and #37953 explicitly does not address it — its own PR description states reasoning items "come back unsigned" and are never replayed with `encrypted_content`.

**Root cause:** OpenAI's prompt cache for reasoning models requires the *exact* prior-turn reasoning item to be either (1) replayed verbatim via `input` with its `encrypted_content`, or (2) chained via `previous_response_id` (server-side, OpenAI holds the state). Anthropic's own protocol correctly drops `thinking` blocks from conversation history once a turn completes — real Claude models don't need them replayed, since Claude's own server-side caching never depended on the client resending them. But that means the bridge has nothing from the client to replay to OpenAI. `#37953` fixed the *shape* of the round-trip (reasoning item vs. flattened text) but did not add `encrypted_content` request/replay or `previous_response_id` chaining, so OpenAI never receives anything it can use to continue the cache — even on a version containing that fix.

**Expected:** cache tokens on a reasoning model behind this bridge should compound turn-over-turn the same way they already do for a real Anthropic Claude model behind the same proxy.
**Actual:** cache tokens stay at (or near) zero on every single turn.

## User Flow

A developer runs Claude Code against a LiteLLM proxy in front of an OpenAI reasoning model, with extended thinking enabled, and has a multi-turn conversation.

### Before a (hypothetical) fix — cache never engages

1. The user starts Claude Code with `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` pointing at the proxy and a reasoning model selected. They ask a question that needs extended thinking.
2. Claude Code sends `POST https://<proxy>/v1/messages` with `"thinking": {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 4000}` and the user's message.
3. A `200` comes back with a `thinking` block followed by a `text` reply; Claude Code shows "Thought for Ns" on screen, then the answer. The response body's `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` is `0` — expected, since there's nothing to cache yet on turn 1.
4. The user asks a related follow-up in the same session. Claude Code sends a second `POST https://<proxy>/v1/messages`, replaying the prior conversation per Anthropic's protocol (the `thinking` block from turn 1 is not resent — only the visible reply and any tool activity are replayed, exactly as a real Claude client behaves).
5. A `200` comes back with a new `thinking` block and answer. `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` in this response is again `0` — identical to a completely fresh conversation, even though the bulk of turn 2's input is identical to turn 1's.
6. The user continues the conversation for 10+ turns. `cache_read_input_tokens` stays at `0` (or negligible) on every single turn. Their usage/billing dashboard shows every turn priced as a full cold request — the discount for repeated context never appears, no matter how long the session runs.

### After a (hypothetical) fix — cache engages like it does for Claude

1. Same setup: user starts Claude Code against the proxy, reasoning model selected, asks a question needing extended thinking.
2. Same first `POST https://<proxy>/v1/messages` — same `200` response, `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` is `0` on turn 1 (still expected — nothing to cache yet).
3. User asks the same follow-up. Claude Code sends the same second `POST https://<proxy>/v1/messages`, replaying history the same way (no client-side change needed).
4. The `200` response's `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` is now **greater than zero**, tracking the size of the shared prefix from turn 1 (including the previously invisible reasoning). The billed cost for turn 2 reflects the cached-token discount.
5. Across a 10+ turn session, `cache_read_input_tokens` keeps growing turn-over-turn, matching how the same proxy already behaves for this same user's conversations against a real Anthropic Claude model.

## Proof the bug occurs

Verified on a real multi-turn conversation with a `gpt-5.6`-family OpenAI reasoning model, accessed through this bridge from Claude Code, at litellm `v1.98.0`. Checked two independent ways: litellm's own debug logs, and a separate wire-level capture of the traffic actually reaching `api.openai.com`.

- Turn-by-turn `cached_tokens` on the *unpatched* bridge: `0` on every turn, for the entire session — no compounding, regardless of how much of the conversation repeats turn-over-turn. This matches exactly what the root cause predicts: with no `previous_response_id` chaining and no `encrypted_content` replay, every turn is sent as an independent request with nothing for OpenAI's cache to match against.
- After prototyping a proxy-side fix (session-chained `previous_response_id`, described in "Suggested direction" above) on the same setup: `cached_tokens` compounded exactly hop-to-hop across 4 turns (`0 → 10124 → 10794 → 11245`), and each `previous_response_id` sent upstream was byte-identical to the prior turn's real response id. A 4th turn asking to summarize the whole conversation, with no other context given, correctly recalled all 3 prior turns — confirming the chained reasoning state was genuinely being used by the model, not just accepted without effect.

We're not including the raw debug-log/packet-capture output itself here, but the measurement above is real and reproducible with the reproduction steps and User Flow described earlier in this issue — happy to run the repro fresh at a maintainer's request if the aggregate numbers aren't enough to act on.

## What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

## What LiteLLM version are you on?

v1.98.0

## Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a well-documented behavioral bug in the Anthropic /v1/messages → OpenAI Responses API bridge: prompt caching for reasoning tokens never engages across turns because encrypted_content/previous_response_id chaining is missing, contrary to expected caching behavior (and behavior seen with real Claude models via the same proxy). It's not a missing feature request in the classic sense — it's documented/expected functionality (cache continuity) that silently fails, causing real cost/billing impact for users of reasoning models behind the bridge. This affects a widely-used integration path (OpenAI reasoning models via Claude Code bridge) and impacts cost accounting, which fits "bug" per the rules (incorrect cost/token accounting, misbehaving integration). No workaround is stated for the affected user besides a custom prototype patch, and it affects the shared core bridging path for reasoning models, so severity is elevated. This is not simply a single narrow provider path—it affects the general reasoning-model caching mechanism, which is significant enough to be P1. Given the complexity (interacting with previous fix #37953, requires design decision on chaining strategy via previous_response_id vs encrypted_content), and given it's a nontrivial architectural fix needing maintainer judgement, needs_human should be true.

items.title: [Bug]: least-busy starves deployments — response-cache hits drift the counter negative, ties always pick the first, and the counter isn't shared across workers
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

This is a root-cause follow-up to #25323, which is open since 2026-04-08 and was nearly auto-closed as stale. That report says traffic "gradually drops to zero" for some deployments but does not identify what makes the counter drift in the first place. This issue names a **deterministic, non-race trigger** (a response-cache hit), plus a second, independent bias that survives any clamp, and a third reason the counter is not actually shared across workers. All three are reproduced below on **1.99.0** (current PyPI) and verified present in `main`.

### What happened?

With `routing_strategy: least-busy` and three healthy deployments in one model group, traffic pins itself to a single deployment for long stretches, then jumps to a different one. Over 24h on our proxy: 689 / 785 / 82 requests across three equal-purpose upstreams, with individual hours as lopsided as 195 / 0 / 5. No cooldowns, no failures, `litellm_deployment_state` clean throughout — the upstreams were all healthy the whole time.

There are three separate defects behind this. The first is the trigger, the second makes the "obvious" fix insufficient, and the third explains why a shared Redis cache does not help.

---

#### 1. A response-cache hit decrements the counter without a matching increment

`LeastBusyLoggingHandler` increments in `log_pre_api_call` and decrements in the success/failure callbacks. A cache hit never calls the LLM, so `log_pre_api_call` never runs — but `caching_handler.py` still dispatches the success callbacks with `cache_hit=True`:

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/main/litellm/caching/caching_handler.py#L691-L706

So the decrement fires alone. This is **not** a race: it is one guaranteed `-1` per cache hit. Anyone running `cache: true` together with `least-busy` drifts negative at a rate proportional to their cache hit rate.

Then, in `_get_available_deployments`, unused deployments are seeded to `0`, so a negative count always wins the `min()` and never recovers — every later request goes to the same deployment, whose counter only sinks further on the next cache hit:

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/main/litellm/router_strategy/least_busy.py#L155-L185

#### 2. Even at zero drift, ties always resolve to the first deployment

`if v < min_traffic` is a strict comparison over `dict` iteration order, so when all counts are equal — which is the normal state under light traffic, and the state you land in *if* the counter is clamped at 0 — the first-listed deployment wins every time. #38746 measured 30/30 requests landing on one deployment with two identical upstreams.

This matters for the fix: **clamping alone converts "always the drifted deployment" into "always the first deployment."** Both are total starvation. #25325 and #34444 clamp only; #25393 and #38746 also address the tie-break. The clamp and the tie-break have to land together.

#### 3. The counter is not shared across workers, despite a Redis cache

`Router` builds its cache without an in-memory TTL:

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/main/litellm/router.py#L776-L778

`DualCache.async_get_cache` returns the in-memory tier first and only falls through to Redis when it misses, and `InMemoryCache.default_ttl` is 600s. `InMemoryCache.set_cache` calls `allow_ttl_override`, which refuses to change a live key's expiry, so repeated increments never shorten it. With `--num_workers 2` each worker therefore routes off its own private counter for up to 10 minutes while overwriting the other's value in Redis. Observed live, same key, seconds apart:

```
{"30950da0(A)": -9, "0fdc2169(B)": 0, "f499c2e9(C)": 0}
{"0fdc2169(B)": -8, "30950da0(A)": 0, "f499c2e9(C)": 0}   <- the other gunicorn worker
```

Docs present `least-busy` + `redis_host` as the way to coordinate in-flight counts across workers, so this is a silent gap between documented and actual behavior.

### Steps to Reproduce

No network access needed — the upstreams are `mock_response`.

```python
import asyncio
import litellm
from litellm import Router


async def main() -> None:
    litellm.cache = litellm.Cache(type="local")

    router = Router(
        model_list=[
            {"model_name": "grp",
             "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/fake-a", "api_key": "x", "mock_response": "ok"},
             "model_info": {"id": "A"}},
            {"model_name": "grp",
             "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/fake-b", "api_key": "x", "mock_response": "ok"},
             "model_info": {"id": "B"}},
        ],
        routing_strategy="least-busy",
        cache_responses=True,
    )

    key = "grp_request_count"
    msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": "same prompt every time"}]

    for i in range(6):  # 1 miss + 5 hits
        await router.acompletion(model="grp", messages=msgs, max_tokens=4, temperature=0)
        await asyncio.sleep(0.3)  # let the async logging worker drain
        print(f"after call {i + 1}: {await router.cache.async_get_cache(key=key)}")

    picked: dict[str, int] = {}
    for _ in range(20):
        d = await router.async_get_available_deployment(
            model="grp", request_kwargs={}, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "new"}]
        )
        picked[d["model_info"]["id"]] = picked.get(d["model_info"]["id"], 0) + 1
    print("20 selections:", picked)


asyncio.run(main())
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
$ pip install litellm==1.99.0 && python repro.py
after call 1: {'A': 0}
after call 2: {'A': -1, 'B': 0}
after call 3: {'A': -2, 'B': 0}
after call 4: {'A': -3, 'B': 0}
after call 5: {'A': -4, 'B': 0}
after call 6: {'A': -5, 'B': 0}

counter: {'A': -5, 'B': 0}
20 selections: {'A': 20}          # expected ~10/10
```

Defect 3, same version:

```shell
litellm.default_in_memory_ttl  : None
DualCache.default_in_memory_ttl: None
InMemoryCache.default_ttl      : 600 seconds
ttl unchanged by later writes  : True
```

### Expected behaviour

1. A cache hit should not decrement a counter that was never incremented — the counter should track in-flight upstream calls only.
2. With all counts equal, selection should spread across the tied deployments rather than always returning the first.
3. With `redis_host` configured, the in-flight counter should be shared across workers rather than served from a 600s-stale per-process copy.

### Suggested fix

The three defects need three changes, and 1+2 must ship together or starvation simply moves:

1. Skip the decrement when the callback is a cache hit (`kwargs.get("cache_hit") is True`), or gate the whole handler on it. Clamping with `max(v - 1, 0)` is a useful backstop for genuine races but treats the symptom here.
2. Collect all ids tied at the minimum and `random.choice` among them — the approach in #25393 / #38746.
3. Have `Router` pass an explicit short `default_in_memory_ttl` (or read the counter with `local_only=False`) so the shared tier is authoritative when Redis is configured.

There are currently **five open PRs against this one function** — #25325, #25393, #34444, #38746, #38910 — the oldest open since April. None is merged, and none covers all three defects. I'm happy to open a PR combining 1+2 (+3 separately, since it touches `Router`) if a maintainer indicates which of the existing PRs to build on rather than adding a sixth. Please say which and I'll rebase onto it.

### Are you a ML Ops Team?

No

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.99.0 (also reproduced on 1.98.0; `least_busy.py`, `dual_cache.py` and `in_memory_cache.py` are byte-identical to `main` at time of filing)

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a well-documented, reproducible bug report identifying three concrete root causes in the least-busy routing strategy: (1) cache hits triggering a decrement without a matching increment causing counters to drift negative and never recover, (2) strict tie-breaking always favoring the first deployment even when counters are clamped, and (3) the in-memory TTL cache preventing proper cross-worker coordination via Redis. The behavior clearly violates the documented/expected contract of least-busy routing (even distribution across healthy deployments), and a full reproduction script with clear before/after evidence is provided. This is a regression-adjacent, core-routing-path defect affecting a widely-used strategy (least-busy) combined with a widely-used feature (caching) and multi-worker deployments — this is a shared core path affecting many users, not a narrow edge case. It causes real production traffic imbalance/starvation with no viable workaround (cache must be disabled to avoid it, defeating the purpose of caching). Given the "many providers or shared core path affected" modifier, urgency should be raised one level from what might otherwise be P2 to P1. It is not a security issue, not a docs-only issue (docs correctly describe intended behavior, but code violates it), and it's not a feature request — it's behavior violating the documented contract, so it's bug. Given the severity (P1) and that it bundles three distinct defects requiring judgement on how to prioritize/fix, this needs human maintainer attention to confirm scope and coordinate the three fixes together as noted by the reporter.

items.title: [Bug]: POST /v1/chat/completions with model a2a/{agent} bypasses   object_permission.agents scope checks
items.body:
## Describe the bug
  Virtual keys with `object_permission.agents` scoped to one agent are
  denied on native A2A routes but allowed on OpenAI-compatible chat
  completions for a different agent.
  **Expected:** A key scoped to agent A returns 403 on both:
  - `POST /a2a/{agent_b}/message/send`
  - `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `"model": "a2a/{agent_b}"`
  **Observed:**
  - Key scoped to agent B only → `POST /a2a/agent_a/message/send` → 403
  (correct)
  - Same key → `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `model: a2a/agent_a` →
  200 (incorrect)
  Native `/a2a/*` calls `AgentRequestHandler.is_agent_allowed()` in
  `litellm/proxy/agent_endpoints/a2a_endpoints.py`. OpenAI mode appears
  to route through `llm_router` in `litellm/proxy/route_llm_request.py`
  before `route_a2a_agent_request()` runs the same check (when
  `pattern_router` / router fallthrough matches `a2a/*` models).
  **Impact:** Clients using OpenAI chat mode can invoke agents outside
  their key allowlist even when native A2A correctly enforces scope.
  ## Relevant log output
  N/A — authorization failure expected but request succeeds with 200 on
  chat completions path.
  ## Are you a LiteLLM user or a LiteLLM developer
  - [x] LiteLLM user
  ## LiteLLM version
  Observed on LiteLLM proxy **1.95.0** (local Docker). Likely affects any
  deployment where `a2a/{agent}` models route via `llm_router` before
  `route_a2a_agent_request`.
  ## Steps to reproduce
  1. Register two native upstream agents (e.g. `agent_a`, `agent_b`) via
  `POST /v1/agents`.
  2. Note each agent's **agent_id UUID** from `GET /v1/agents`
  (`object_permission.agents` uses UUIDs, not `agent_name`).
  3. Mint virtual keys via `POST /key/generate`:
     - Key A: `object_permission.agents: [<agent_a_id>]`
     - Key B: `object_permission.agents: [<agent_b_id>]`
  4. Control: Key A → `POST /a2a/agent_a/message/send` → 200
  5. Native (passes): Key B → `POST /a2a/agent_a/message/send` → 403
  6. Bug: Key B → `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `model: a2a/agent_a` →
  403 expected, 200 observed
  ## Suspected code
  - `litellm/proxy/route_llm_request.py` — permission check in
  `route_a2a_agent_request()` may run too late (after `llm_router` /
  `pattern_router` fallthrough)
  - `litellm/proxy/agent_endpoints/a2a_routing.py` — has
  `is_agent_allowed` check but not reached on chat path
  ## Context (optional)
  Related: #25421, PRs #36221 / #36020 (native path hardening). This
  report is specifically the OpenAI chat completions entry point.

gold.rationale: This is an authorization bypass: a virtual key scoped to a specific agent via object_permission.agents can access a different, unauthorized agent through the OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions endpoint, even though the same check correctly blocks it on the native /a2a/* endpoint. This is a real access-control bypass with a plausible exploit path (unauthorized agent invocation), so it takes precedence as security over bug. It affects the shared core routing path (llm_router) used by all OpenAI-compatible chat completions calls to a2a models, which raises severity. No workaround is mentioned (native endpoint works but that's not a workaround for chat completions clients), so this is widely impactful for any deployment using a2a with scoped permissions - P0/P1 territory. Given it's an auth bypass affecting the core router path, I'll set P0. Security issues and P0/P1 issues always require human judgement to confirm reproduction and assess fix approach.

items.title: [Bug]: Background health check sends `supports_max_reasoning_effort` as a request field to Bedrock (400), for models without `supports_*_reasoning_effort` in the model map
items.body:
### What happened?

With `general_settings.background_health_checks: true`, `/health` reports a Bedrock Claude deployment as unhealthy. Bedrock returns **400** with:

```
{"message":"supports_max_reasoning_effort: Extra inputs are not permitted"}
```

`supports_max_reasoning_effort` is a **capability flag**, not a request parameter — it looks like it is leaking from the model metadata into the request body, but only on the health-check code path.

**The same deployment serves normal traffic fine.** Over 24h it handled 194 requests via `/chat/completions` with no occurrence of this error.

### What makes it a health-check-path issue

I reproduced the health-check payload through the normal completion path against the *same* deployment. All three succeed:

| Request via `/v1/chat/completions` | Result |
|---|---|
| `{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}` | 200 OK |
| same + `"max_tokens": 10` | 200 OK |
| `{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"test from litellm"}], "max_tokens": 10}` (mirrors the health-check payload) | 200 OK |
| **actual background health check on the same model** | **400** |

Same model, same deployment config, same effective payload — only the code path differs.

### What distinguishes an affected model

Two Bedrock Anthropic deployments in the same proxy, configured identically (both set `thinking`, `drop_params: true`, `additional_drop_params`):

| `model_info` field | affected model | unaffected sibling |
|---|---|---|
| `supports_max_reasoning_effort` | `None` | `True` |
| `supports_xhigh_reasoning_effort` | `None` | `True` |
| `bedrock_output_config_effort_ceiling` | `None` | `xhigh` |

Only the one **without** these flags fails. There is a related warning emitted for that same model:

```
anthropic_claude3_transformation.py:761 - Bedrock Invoke: stripping unsupported `output_config`
for model=<model> — neither `supports_output_config` nor any `supports_*_reasoning_effort`
flag is set in model_prices_and_context_window.json.
```

So the failure appears to be in the branch taken when those capability flags are absent.

### Relevant log output

```
litellm.BadRequestError: BedrockException - {"message":"supports_max_reasoning_effort: Extra inputs are not permitted"}
stack trace: Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../litellm/llms/custom_httpx/llm_http_handler.py", line 254, in _make_common_async_call
    response = await async_httpx_client.post(
  File ".../litellm/litellm_core_utils/logging_utils.py", line 289, in async_wrapper
    result = await func(*args, **kwargs)
  File ".../litellm/llms/custom_httpx/http_handler.py", line 667, in post
    await _raise_masked_async_error(e, stream)
  File ".../litellm/llms/custom_httpx/http_handler.py", line 454, in _raise_masked_async_error
    raise MaskedHTTPStatusError(e, message=_text, text=_text) from None
litellm.llms.custom_httpx.http_handler.MaskedHTTPStatusError: Client error '400 Bad Request'
for url 'https://bedrock-runtime.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/...'
```

Note the request does reach Bedrock — this is AWS rejecting the field, not client-side validation.

### Why it matters

The model is healthy and serving production traffic, but shows permanently red on `/health` and on any dashboard built on it. A health signal that is wrong on your busiest model trains people to ignore it.

### Impact / workaround

No good workaround. Setting the capability flags would silence it, but that means asserting a model capability we have not verified — papering over the symptom with a possibly false claim.

### What LiteLLM version are you on?

v1.93.0 (`LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True`), Python 3.13, provider `bedrock`, region `us-west-2`, deployed via the proxy on Kubernetes.

gold.rationale: A clear, well-reproduced bug: the background health-check code path leaks the `supports_max_reasoning_effort` capability flag into the actual Bedrock request body, causing a 400 error, only when the model lacks certain reasoning-effort/output_config flags in the model cost map. The production traffic path handles the same payload fine, isolating the bug to the health-check code path (likely a difference in how request params are built/stripped). This is a regression-like behavioral defect (code violates expected contract: capability flags should never be sent as request params) rather than a docs or question issue. It's not security. It affects health-check reporting broadly for any Bedrock model missing these flags, which could affect many users' monitoring/dashboards, but doesn't break actual serving traffic — there's an explicit workaround noted (setting the flags) though the reporter considers it a hack, so a real workaround exists. Given a subset of models/paths affected (health-check only, not chat completions) and a stated workaround, this should be P2 lowered from a potentially higher severity, but health checks feeding dashboards that many rely on for monitoring is not user-facing breakage of core functionality, so P2 fits well with a documented workaround lowering severity further, but I'll keep at P2 given clear reproduction and specificity of the affected code path. This is a well-specified, reproducible bug with clear steps and stack trace, so a maintainer doesn't need to triage for more info — it can be routed directly to the bedrock/health-check module owners.
